name: Graphs
description: Visual way to show relationships between two quantities

content.overview: Ever look at a table full of numbers and just... glaze over? Yeah, same. That's exactly why graphs exist. A graph takes those numbers and turns them into a picture, so instead of squinting at a list, you just glance and go "oh, I see what's happening." {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Here's the thing about graphs: they let you SEE a relationship instead of hunting for it in a pile of numbers. {{viz:chart-01}}

Think about a road trip. You could write down "at 1 hour we'd gone 60 km, at 2 hours 120 km, at 3 hours 180 km"... or you could just plot those points and instantly see you're moving at a steady pace. That's the whole magic trick.

The setup is simple: two axes, usually called x and y. Every point on the graph is just a pair of values living together — like "at time x = 5 seconds, position y = 20 meters." One dot, two pieces of information.

**Why you'll come to love graphs:**
- You spot patterns in about half a second
- A straight line? Simple, steady relationship
- A curve? Something more interesting is going on
- Steep = changing fast
- Flat = barely changing at all

**The graph types you'll bump into in physics:**
- **Line graphs** — distance vs. time, temperature vs. time, that kind of thing
- **Scatter plots** — real-world data points that don't connect perfectly (because real life is messy)
- **Bar graphs** — great for comparing separate quantities side by side
- **Curved graphs** — for when the relationship isn't so simple {{viz:anim-01}}

So don't think of a graph as "extra math homework." Think of it as a translator — it takes boring numbers and makes them talk to you.
keyPoints: Graphs turn numbers into a picture you can actually read at a glance
X-axis runs horizontal, Y-axis runs vertical — that's your stage
A straight line means a simple, linear relationship
A curve means things are changing in a more complicated way
Steepness tells you how fast something's changing
Once you can read a graph, patterns just jump out at you
content.whyItMatters: You're going to run into graphs constantly — every physics textbook, every lab report, every research paper leans on them to tell its story. Get comfortable reading them now, and a huge chunk of physics gets easier overnight.
